holding_summary: The Supreme Court reversed an injunction and held that an automobile tourist court is not a nuisance per se as a matter of law, even in a strictly residential, unzoned area, because absent proof of an actual nuisance in fact the owner has a constitutional right to use land for any lawful purpose.

quotes.text: We, therefore, hold that an Automobile Tourist Court or Inn is not a nuisance per se, even in a strictly residential area which is unrestricted and unzoned.
Such owners possess a constitutional right to use their land for any lawful purpose.

notes: characterization left null: the court's holding addresses nuisance/zoning law, not the legal classification (lease/license/lodging/innkeeping) of the guest occupancy itself.

court: Adams County Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: The court held that a lease covenant restricting use of the premises to 'a motel and for no other purpose' was not necessarily violated as a matter of law by renting some units for extended off-season periods as housekeeping units, reasoning that motels, like hotels and tourist lodging houses, may accommodate both transient and semi-permanent guests without losing their essential character, and that the lease did not expressly restrict occupancy to transients only.

quotes.text: The basic concept of a motel is that it furnishes a type of accommodations for the traveling public having some, but not all, of the attributes of a hotel and some, but not all, of the attributes of a tourist lodging house.
Doing so does not destroy the basic character of the hotel or the tourist lodging house as being primarily designed to accommodate transient guests.
Had the lessors desired to restrict the use of the premises solely to transient guests they could easily have done so by a similar restriction.

holding_summary: The Superior Court affirmed a summary conviction for violating a zoning ordinance prohibiting transient or temporary residential occupancy of trailers and cabins in a commercially-zoned area, holding that occasional living use of trailers, incidental to defendant's trailer sales and repair business, did not establish a valid nonconforming use of the land for a rental lodging business.

quotes.text: The entire sense of the testimony is that the living by people in trailers on defendant’s property, with the exception, perhaps, of his son, was purely incidental to the defendant’s business of selling new and used trailers and repairing trailers. Renting living quarters was not the defendant’s business and there is not even any effort to assert that such was the case.
“Cabins, including any and all structures designed for temporary or transient occupancy as living or sleeping quarters”

notes: characterization left null: the record affirmatively establishes there was no letting-for-pay arrangement at issue, only incidental trailer occupancy; who_was_letting is 'unclear' for the same reason.

notes: Case treats a tenant's subletting of rooms to individual roomers as an unremarkable, lawful commercial arrangement; the actual holding concerns landlord tort liability, not the legality of the letting itself.

court: Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas
notes: Case concerns constitutionality of a transient-retail-merchant licensing tax on a seasonal toy store; 'transient boarders' appears only in a dictionary definition quoted for statutory construction, unrelated to lodging.

court: Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: Construing a residential zoning ordinance's use-district exception permitting 'the renting of rooms or lodgings or the serving of meals for compensation,' the court held that tourist homes and coffee houses fall squarely within that exception, and dismissed a mandamus action seeking to compel the borough to enforce the zoning ordinance against them.

quotes.text: It is our opinion that tourist homes and coffee houses of the type generally referred to by counsel for the parties fall under the head of “Use District Exceptions” by the provision, “In the residence districts the use regulations shall not be held to prevent the renting of rooms or lodgings or the serving of meals for compensation.”
Certainly tourist homes involve “the renting of rooms or lodgings,” and “the serving of meals for compensation,” and it seems to us that is all they do involve.

Premises-liability case about a landlord's duty to maintain a common areaway in a multi-tenant building; does not address compensated short-term occupancy or its regulation.

holding_summary: The court held that a deed covenant permitting only 'not more than two dwelling houses, to be used as dwellings only, and for no other purpose' barred the grantee from erecting sleeping cottages rented overnight to tourists, because such transient lodging use is not a 'dwelling house' use and directly competes with the grantor's reserved tourists'-home business.

quotes.text: We therefore hold that the language “for the erection of not more than two dwelling houses to be used as dwellings only, and for no other purpose or purposes” is sufficiently clear, explicit and definite to restrict the use of sleeping cottages on the land in question.
The use by defendants of sleeping cottages would clearly not be a use for a dwelling house and would be in direct competition and conflict with the use of the tourists’ home by plaintiff.
she conducted what is commonly known as a tourists’ home, for keeping overnight guests and serving meals

notes: Mixed: the court enforces and thereby validates the grantor's short-term tourist-lodging business as a legitimate protectable enterprise (favorable), while simultaneously barring the grantee's competing sleeping cottages for transient guests (adverse to that particular short-term letting use).
